Situation1: A family member has a significant event they want to share with everyone.
Expectation2: Observe kosher dietary laws in daily meals
Situation2: While traveling, only a small vendor known to be kosher-certified is within reach for the next meal.
Story:
I was so excited to visit my daughter and her family after months apart. My grandson, Daniel, had been practicing for his school play for weeks, and tonight was the big performance. The whole family planned to celebrate afterward at a nearby restaurant, a place Daniel had chosen because he loves their famous burgers. As a grandparent, I wanted nothing more than to be there, to laugh and share in Daniel’s joy, to make memories with everyone.

But as we walked toward the restaurant, my heart tightened. I knew this place wasn’t kosher, and the only kosher vendor in the area was a small stand a few blocks away, closing soon. My family expected me to join them, to be part of the celebration, but my faith called me to keep kosher, as I always have. I could see Daniel’s hopeful face, my daughter’s warm smile, and I felt the weight of their expectations. At the same time, I felt the pull of my own beliefs, the quiet voice reminding me of who I am. I stood on the sidewalk, torn, the laughter of my family drifting ahead as I wrestled with what to do.
